title: When Can Unlabeled Data Pools Replace Membership Queries?

paper.title: When Can Unlabeled Data Pools Replace Membership Queries?
paper.abstract:
Abstract Membership queries let a learner label arbitrary points and give near-optimal O ~ ​ ( n ​ log ⁡ ( 1 / ε ) ) \tilde{O}(n\log(1/\varepsilon)) label complexity for halfspaces under every marginal. A pool learner may label only sampled points. We ask when unlabeled data can replace membership queries. For homogeneous halfspaces the answer depends only on the angular law of X / ‖ X ‖ X/\|X\| . If this law assigns zero mass to every hyperplane through the origin and positive mass to every nonempty open set of directions together with its reflection, a pool learner uses O ⁡ ( n ​ log 3 ​ n ​ log ⁡ ( n / ( ε ​ δ ) ) ) O(n\log^{3}n\log(n/(\varepsilon\delta))) labels, uniformly over all such marginals and targets, without density, moment, concavity or isotropy assumptions. The same label bound holds for non-homogeneous halfspaces under every marginal with full support and no mass on affine hyperplanes, including Gaussians.
Dropping either angular assumption admits Ω ⁡ ( 1 / ε ) \Omega(1/\varepsilon) pool versus O ⁡ ( log ⁡ ( 1 / ε ) ) O(\log(1/\varepsilon)) membership-query separations, even with unlimited unlabeled data. The price is paid in unlabeled data: in dimension n ≥ 3 n\geq 3 , for every unlabeled budget fixed in advance, some marginal satisfying both assumptions forces Ω ⁡ ( 1 / ε ) \Omega(1/\varepsilon) labels.
For isotropic s s -concave marginals in dimension n ≥ 3 n\geq 3 , unlimited pools keep logarithmic label rates for every finite s s . With an unlabeled budget fixed in advance, class-uniform polylogarithmic rates hold exactly for s > − 1 / ( n + 1 ) s>-1/(n+1) , or s > − 1 / n s>-1/n under central symmetry, and in the general class the optimal rate between these thresholds is Θ ~ ( ε − ( n − 2 ) / n ) \tilde{\Theta}(\varepsilon^{-(n-2)/n}) . This extends the range s ≥ − 1 / ( 2 n + 3 ) s\geq-1/(2n+3) of previous sample-based guarantees, in the realizable setting.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Membership queries are an unusually powerful form of active learning. The learner may choose any point and ask for its label. For halfspaces, point location , which labels every point of a given finite set under an unknown halfspace, can be done for a passive sample of size N N with O ⁡ ( n ​ log 2 ​ n ​ log ⁡ N ) O(n\log^{2}n\log N) synthesized queries ( Hopkins et al., 2020b ) , giving near-optimal membership-query learning under every marginal. An ordinary pool learner may only request labels of points it has sampled, and on worst-case finite point sets this can require Ω ⁡ ( N ) \Omega(N) labels ( Dasgupta, 2004 , Black et al., 2026 ) . For affine halfspaces under Gaussian marginals and a pool of m m points, Diakonikolas et al. (2024) prove an information-theoretic Ω ~ ​ ( n / ( ε ​ log ⁡ m ) ) \tilde{\Omega}(n/(\varepsilon\log m)) lower bound. We ask the following distributional question (ignoring computational hardness). For which marginals can an unlabeled pool substitute for synthesized membership queries without increasing label complexity? We count two resources separately, namely labels and unlabeled examples , the latter meaning every sampled point the learner inspects. For halfspaces through the origin x ↦ sign ⁡ ⟨ w , x ⟩ x\mapsto\operatorname{sign}\langle w,x\rangle only the direction of a point matters, so the relevant object is the angular law μ = ℒ ⁡ ( X / ‖ X ‖ ) \mu=\mathcal{L}(X/\|X\|) , the distribution of the direction of X X .

sections.heading: 1.1 Summary of Results
sections.text: Theorem 1.1 (Pools match membership queries in labels, Theorem 3.7 ) . Let n ≥ 2 n\geq 2 and let D D have no atom at the origin and an angular law that is hyperplane-null (it gives probability zero to every hyperplane through the origin) and has symmetric full support (every nonempty open set O O of directions has μ ⁡ ( O ∪ − O ) > 0 \mu(O\cup-O)>0 , which holds in particular if every nonempty open set of directions has positive probability, Section 2.2 ). A pool learner achieves error ε \varepsilon with probability 1 − δ 1-\delta using O ⁡ ( n ​ log 3 ​ n ​ log ⁡ n ε ​ δ ) O\Bigl(n\log^{3}n\,\log\frac{n}{\varepsilon\delta}\Bigr) labels, uniformly over all such D D and all targets. This matches the Ω ⁡ ( n ​ log ⁡ ( 1 / ε ) ) \Omega(n\log(1/\varepsilon)) lower bound under the uniform distribution up to a log 3 ⁡ n \log^{3}n factor. The number of unlabeled examples is finite almost surely, necessarily depends on D D ( Theorem 1.3 ), and for our simulation is exponential in n n even for the uniform distribution ( Remark 3.11 ). Like the lower bounds below, Theorem 1.1 is information-theoretic. It counts labels and unlabeled examples, not running time ( Section C.2 ). The two assumptions can also be placed on different distributions. Error can be measured under a hyperplane-null law while labels come from points of a second law with symmetric full support, which may be atomic. The evaluation law itself must remain hyperplane-null ( Theorem 3.8 ). A simpler learner, directional search , approximates each membership query at a fixed angular resolution. It uses O ⁡ ( n ​ log ⁡ ( n / ρ μ − 1 ​ ( ε / 16 ) ) ) O(n\log(n/\rho_{\mu}^{-1}(\varepsilon/16))) labels, where ρ μ − 1 ​ ( ε ) \rho_{\mu}^{-1}(\varepsilon) is the largest width θ \theta such that every band { u : | ⟨ u , w ⟩ | < θ } \{u:|\langle u,w\rangle|<\theta\} has μ \mu -mass at most ε \varepsilon ( Proposition 3.12 ). A mixture of three centered Gaussians makes this procedure’s label count arbitrarily large at fixed ε \varepsilon , even after an invertible linear change of coordinates ( Example 3.13 ). In contrast, Theorem 1.1 estimates query precision from unlabeled data and uses robust point location to confine its marginal dependence to the unlabeled cost. Theorem 1.2 (Both angular assumptions are necessary, Propositions 4.1 and 4.2 ) . For every ε \varepsilon there are two marginals, each depending on ε \varepsilon , for which every pool learner needs Ω ⁡ ( 1 / ε ) \Omega(1/\varepsilon) labels even with unlimited unlabeled data, while membership queries need O ⁡ ( log ⁡ ( 1 / ε ) ) O(\log(1/\varepsilon)) . The first is a smooth, centrally symmetric, hyperplane-null marginal on ℝ 3 \mathbb{R}^{3} without symmetric full support, with a finite family of targets. The second is a full-support marginal on ℝ 4 \mathbb{R}^{4} that charges a hyperplane, with a family of targets containing arbitrarily small tilts of one target, and there the lower bound holds in expectation. When both assumptions hold, pools recover the membership-query label rate, but the number of unlabeled examples in Theorem 1.1 depends on the marginal, and this dependence is unavoidable. Theorem 1.3 (Unlabeled cost cannot be uniform, Proposition 4.3 ) . Let n ≥ 3 n\geq 3 . For every unlabeled budget U ⁡ ( ε ) U(\varepsilon) , some marginal with a smooth, everywhere-positive, centrally symmetric density, so that both angular assumptions hold, forces every pool learner that inspects at most U ⁡ ( ε ) U(\varepsilon) examples to use Ω ⁡ ( 1 / ε ) \Omega(1/\varepsilon) labels, information-theoretically. For fixed n n this is the passive rate. Here the hard distribution may depend on the budget and on ε \varepsilon . We do not claim that a single distribution defeats every finite pool. Together with Theorem 1.1 , this shows that labels admit a bound uniform over the marginal class, whereas the number of unlabeled examples does not. Inside structured classes the same mechanism gives refined exponents. When homogeneous halfspaces act on a high-probability core as affine halfspaces of a lower-dimensional ball ( Definition 4.4 ), every finite budget forces Ω n ( ε − ( n − 2 ) / n ) \Omega_{n}(\varepsilon^{-(n-2)/n}) labels ( Theorem 4.5 ), which is tight for s s -concave marginals with − 1 / n < s ≤ − 1 / ( n + 1 ) -1/n<s\leq-1/(n+1) ( Section 5 ). Theorem 1.4 ( s s -concave marginals, Section 5 ) . For isotropic (mean zero, identity covariance) s s -concave marginals in dimension n ≥ 3 n\geq 3 ( Definition 5.1 , where s = 0 s=0 is log-concavity, and more negative s s allows heavier tails): (i) with an unlimited pool, O ⁡ ( n ​ log 3 ​ n ​ log ⁡ ( n / ( ε ​ δ ) ) ) O(n\log^{3}n\log(n/(\varepsilon\delta))) labels suffice for every finite s s ( Theorem 3.7 ), compared with the generic Ω ⁡ ( n ​ log ⁡ ( 1 / ε ) ) \Omega(n\log(1/\varepsilon)) lower bound; (ii) with an unlabeled budget fixed in advance for the class, polylogarithmic labels are achievable, via the disagreement-based learner CAL ( Cohn et al., 1994 ) and a class-uniform disagreement bound O n , s ​ ( log ⁡ ( 1 / ε ) ) O_{n,s}(\log(1/\varepsilon)) ( Section 2.3 ), if and only if s > − 1 / ( n + 1 ) s>-1/(n+1) , or s > − 1 / n s>-1/n in the centrally symmetric subclass ( f ⁡ ( x ) = f ⁡ ( − x ) f(x)=f(-x) ); (iii) for − 1 / n < s ≤ − 1 / ( n + 1 ) -1/n<s\leq-1/(n+1) in the general class, the worst-case disagreement coefficient is Θ n , s ( ε − ( n − 2 ) / n ) \Theta_{n,s}(\varepsilon^{-(n-2)/n}) , and Θ ~ n , s ( ε − ( n − 2 ) / n ) \tilde{\Theta}_{n,s}(\varepsilon^{-(n-2)/n}) labels are necessary and sufficient with an unlabeled budget fixed in advance, at constant confidence; (iv) for s ≤ − 1 / n s\leq-1/n both the disagreement coefficient and the label count are Θ ⁡ ( 1 / ε ) \Theta(1/\varepsilon) , even in the symmetric subclass. Constants depend on n n and s s . In regime (ii) we prove no lower bound beyond Ω ⁡ ( n ​ log ⁡ ( 1 / ε ) ) \Omega(n\log(1/\varepsilon)) . All statements concern the realizable setting. Balcan and Zhang (2017) give polynomial-time, noise-tolerant learners for s ≥ − 1 / ( 2 n + 3 ) s\geq-1/(2n+3) . Theorem 1.4 is information-theoretic apart from the CAL implementation ( Corollary D.15 ). It locates the thresholds for class-uniform rates and the sharp rate between them, rather than extending their computational or noise guarantees. Item (i) follows from Theorem 3.7 . Items (ii)–(iv) use CAL and Lemma A.3 , with new arguments for the exponent in (iii) ( Section 5.1 ) and the symmetric construction in (iv) ( Lemma D.26 ).

sections.heading: A target-independent margin scale.
sections.text: A compactness argument implies that hyperplane-nullness is equivalent to the band mass ρ μ ​ ( θ ) = sup ‖ w ‖ = 1 μ ⁡ { u : | ⟨ u , w ⟩ | < θ } \rho_{\mu}(\theta)=\sup_{\|w\|=1}\mu\{u:|\langle u,w\rangle|<\theta\} vanishing with θ \theta ( Lemma 3.1 ). A uniform relative-deviation (VC) bound then finds, from unlabeled data alone, a width θ 0 > 0 \theta_{0}>0 (a margin floor ) with the following property. The learner draws an independent passive sample , an i.i.d. sample of size N = O ~ ​ ( n / ε ) N=\tilde{O}(n/\varepsilon) that it will label in full by point location, so that every consistent halfspace is ε \varepsilon -accurate. With high probability, every passive point has normalized margin at least θ 0 \theta_{0} from the fixed unknown target. No rate at which the band mass ρ μ \rho_{\mu} vanishes is assumed, which is why labels are uniform while precision and unlabeled cost are not. This geometric margin is unrelated to the Tsybakov margin condition on label noise.

sections.heading: Answering queries with pool points.
sections.text: The point-location algorithm of Hopkins et al. (2020b) repeatedly restricts to a subspace V V containing many sample points and applies a linear map T T that puts those points in approximately isotropic position (their second-moment matrix becomes nearly a multiple of the identity). Every such subspace contains a passive point, which lower-bounds the norm of the projected target. Hence a pool point within angle γ \gamma of a requested direction (or of its antipode, with the label negated) returns the correct label unless the transformed query q q has relative margin | ⟨ q , w ′ ⟩ | / ( ‖ q ‖ ​ ‖ w ′ ‖ ) |\langle q,w^{\prime}\rangle|/(\|q\|\|w^{\prime}\|) at most γ ​ κ ​ ( T ) / θ 0 \gamma\kappa(T)/\theta_{0} with respect to the transformed target normal w ′ w^{\prime} , where κ ⁡ ( T ) = ‖ T ‖ ​ ‖ T − 1 ‖ \kappa(T)=\|T\|\|T^{-1}\| is the condition number ( Lemma 3.5 ). Because the learner chooses γ \gamma after seeing T T , the pool answers form a subspace-relative oracle ( Definition 3.4 ). This is stronger than a single margin-tolerant oracle in fixed coordinates, and it is what robust point location needs.

sections.heading: Robust point location.
sections.text: We modify Hopkins et al. (2020b) to tolerate such an oracle. Their margin comparisons already carry multiplicative slack. The one step that needs exact comparisons is deterministic median selection, which we replace by a round-robin tournament robust to near-ties, and we enlarge one acceptance threshold. This costs one log ⁡ n \log n factor ( Proposition 3.6 ). Table 2 lists, with their hypotheses, all results of Hopkins et al. (2020b) that we use.

sections.heading: Hard instances for the lower bounds.
sections.text: The lower bounds place the informative directions in a region of vanishing mass. In the general s s -concave class, a rare tail moves the mean, while a high-probability core is, after a projective change of coordinates, a uniform ball. In the symmetric class, successive logarithmic radial scales are dominated by different norms, so the angular law can approximate a mixture of the angular laws of elongated ellipsoids.

sections.heading: Relation to prior work.
sections.text: The angular law (radially symmetric marginals were already exploited for origin-centered separators by Kearns 1998 ), exponential active improvements, pool-versus-synthesis gaps, and the splitting-index distinction between how informative a query is and how likely the unlabeled distribution is to produce it ( Dasgupta, 2005 , Hanneke, 2014 ) are all classical. That a sufficiently rich pool approximates membership queries is folklore. The infinite full-support pool limit is discussed in Gonen et al. (2013) , and Diakonikolas et al. (2024) remark that pools approach membership queries as they grow exponentially. Dasgupta’s label bounds carry logarithmic factors that depend on the marginal, as does the directional search of Proposition 3.12 . Our contributions are threefold. Theorem 3.7 removes every marginal-dependent factor from the label count. We show that both angular assumptions are needed. Finally, we show that the remaining marginal dependence, in unlabeled data, cannot be removed ( Theorem 1.3 ). Section 7 gives detailed comparisons, including with universal and marginal-nonuniform rates, and separates new arguments from results of prior work.

sections.text: Throughout, O ~ \tilde{O} hides polylogarithmic factors, and subscripts such as O n O_{n} , Ω n \Omega_{n} , O n , s O_{n,s} indicate constants depending only on those parameters.

sections.heading: 2.1 Pool and membership-query models
sections.text: Let h w ​ ( x ) = sign ⁡ ⟨ w , x ⟩ h_{w}(x)=\operatorname{sign}\langle w,x\rangle , w ∈ S n − 1 w\in S^{n-1} , be the class of homogeneous halfspaces, with the convention sign ⁡ ( 0 ) = + 1 \operatorname{sign}(0)=+1 throughout. The target normal is w ⋆ w^{\star} and the target is h ⋆ = h w ⋆ h^{\star}=h_{w^{\star}} . In the membership-query model, the learner may choose any q ∈ ℝ n q\in\mathbb{R}^{n} and request h ⋆ ​ ( q ) h^{\star}(q) . In the ordinary i.i.d. pool model, the learner observes an unlabeled stream X 1 , X 2 , … ∼ D X_{1},X_{2},\ldots\sim D and may request labels only for points that have appeared in that stream. We count label queries and unlabeled examples separately. An unlabeled budget U ⁡ ( ε ) U(\varepsilon) bounds the number of stream elements the learner may inspect, whether or not it requests their labels. For a finite passive sample 𝒳 ⊂ ℝ n \mathcal{X}\subset\mathbb{R}^{n} , point location asks for the labels of all points in 𝒳 \mathcal{X} under an unknown homogeneous halfspace. The synthesized-query algorithm of Hopkins et al. (2020b) uses O ~ ​ ( n ​ log ⁡ | 𝒳 | ) \tilde{O}(n\log|\mathcal{X}|) sign queries. Combined with the standard realizable VC bound, this gives near-optimal membership-query active learning under every marginal.

sections.heading: 3 From a pool to membership queries
sections.text: Hyperplane-nullness gives a target-independent margin scale, and symmetric full support places pool points in every angular cap or its reflection. The robust point location connecting them is summarized in Section 3.3 . Its proof is given in Section 3.4 , with supporting lemmas in Appendix B .

sections.heading: 3.1 A target-independent margin floor
sections.text: A margin floor is a positive scale θ 0 \theta_{0} , computed from unlabeled data without knowledge of the target, such that very little angular probability lies within θ 0 \theta_{0} of any origin-centered hyperplane. ρ μ ​ ( θ 0 ) = sup ‖ w ‖ = 1 Pr Y ∼ μ ⁡ ( | ⟨ w , Y ⟩ | < θ 0 ) ≤ α . \rho_{\mu}(\theta_{0})=\sup_{\|w\|=1}\Pr_{Y\sim\mu}\bigl(|\langle w,Y\rangle|<\theta_{0}\bigr)\leq\alpha. For an independent sample of size N N and any fixed target w ⋆ w^{\star} , a union bound then gives Pr ⁡ ( min j ≤ N ⁡ | ⟨ w ⋆ , Y j ⟩ | < θ 0 ) ≤ N ​ α . \Pr\bigl(\min_{j\leq N}|\langle w^{\star},Y_{j}\rangle|<\theta_{0}\bigr)\leq N\alpha. The floor is not a lower bound on every margin, only a margin scale that holds with high probability for a fixed target. Lemma 3.1 (Uniform anti-concentration) . For n ≥ 2 n\geq 2 , the following are equivalent: μ \mu assigns zero mass to every great subsphere, ρ μ ​ ( θ ) → 0 \rho_{\mu}(\theta)\to 0 as θ \theta decreases to 0 0 , and every n n independent sampled directions are linearly independent almost surely. The computation is finite. Section C.2 gives an explicit implementation in time M 0 O ⁡ ( n ) M_{0}^{O(n)} . Corollary 3.3 (Passive-sample margin floor) . Let 𝒳 \mathcal{X} be an independent passive sample of size N N and let w ⋆ w^{\star} be a fixed unit target normal. With probability at least 1 − δ / 4 1-\delta/4 , every x ∈ 𝒳 x\in\mathcal{X} has normalized margin | ⟨ x , w ⋆ ⟩ | / ‖ x ‖ ≥ θ 0 |\langle x,w^{\star}\rangle|/\|x\|\geq\theta_{0} . Proof. sections.heading: 3.3 Margin-tolerant point location
sections.text: The reduction needs a point-location algorithm that stays correct under the subspace-relative oracle of Definition 3.4 , where queries of very small relative margin in the current transformed instance may receive arbitrary answers.

sections.heading: The algorithm of Hopkins et al. (2020b) in brief.
sections.text: Its weak learner, PartialLearn, labels a constant fraction of a weighted point set ( X , ω ) (X,\omega) with few queries. A boosting loop reweights the unlabeled points and repeats until all of X X is labeled. PartialLearn first finds a subspace V V carrying many points and a linear map T T that puts them in approximately isotropic position . As in Hopkins et al. (2020b) , normalized points ( X , ω ) (X,\omega) in ℝ d \mathbb{R}^{d} are c c -isotropic if ( 1 − c ) / d ≤ 𝔼 ω ​ ⟨ x , v ⟩ 2 ≤ ( 1 + c ) / d (1-c)/d\leq\mathbb{E}_{\omega}\langle x,v\rangle^{2}\leq(1+c)/d for every unit v v . sections.heading: Prior robustness guarantees.
sections.text: The guarantees of Hopkins et al. (2020b) allow the algorithm itself to fail with small probability (their “bounded-error” and “reliable” notions refer to this failure probability), but they assume every query is answered correctly. Their companion work with comparison queries ( Hopkins et al., 2020a ) handles stochastic bounded (Massart) label noise rather than arbitrary answers inside a relative-margin band. The closest model is the unreliable boundary queries of Blum et al. (1995) , where membership queries near the boundary may be answered wrongly and the distribution puts no mass there, but their goal is polynomial-time PAC learning of specific classes rather than near-optimal query complexity for all halfspaces. We are not aware of a near-optimal point-location algorithm with guarantees in this setting. Since a nearby sampled direction can be wrong deterministically, majority votes do not help.

sections.heading: Our modifications.
sections.text: The isotropic-transform arguments of Hopkins et al. (2020b) , which rest on the theorems of Forster (2002) and Barthe (1998) , and their matrix-concentration, structural and boosting arguments do not involve the oracle. Appendix B checks the hypotheses of each result we use under the new oracle. Only three oracle-sensitive steps change. Comparison. | m ⁡ ( a ) | |m(a)| and | m ⁡ ( b ) | |m(b)| are compared via the signs of a a , b b and a signed difference, which is correct whenever the magnitudes differ by more than the tolerance-induced error ( Lemma B.1 ). Selection. Deterministic median selection is fragile under such a comparator, so StructureSearch instead compares all pairs in a small representative set and picks a middle win count, which controls the rank of the selected representative from both sides up to one comparator error ( Lemma B.2 ). This is the classical paired-comparison method in the bounded-error model of Ajtai et al. (2015) , and it costs one extra log ⁡ n \log n factor. Dimension reduction. DimReduce accepts a sampled subset when its representative’s margin is small relative to a scaled reference point, tested with three sign queries, and spurious accepted subsets only add positive semidefinite terms to the covariance estimate ( Hopkins et al., 2020b , Lemma 4.15) . We only enlarge the acceptance threshold so that subsets of small-margin points are still accepted under comparison error ( Lemma B.7 ). Proposition 3.6 (Robust point location) . Let X ⊂ ℝ n X\subset\mathbb{R}^{n} be a set of N N points, none on the target hyperplane. There exists a tolerance η ∗ = n − O ⁡ ( log ⁡ n ) \eta^{*}=n^{-O(\log n)} such that the point-location learner of Hopkins et al. (2020b) , with the modifications of Appendix B and given an η ∗ \eta^{*} -subspace-relative oracle, labels every point of X X correctly with probability at least 1 − δ ′ 1-\delta^{\prime} using O ⁡ ( n ​ log 3 ​ n ​ log ⁡ ( N / δ ′ ) ) O(n\log^{3}n\log(N/\delta^{\prime})) queries. Every instance ( V 0 , T ) (V_{0},T) it queries has V 0 V_{0} containing a point of X X , so P V 0 ​ w ⋆ ≠ 0 P_{V_{0}}w^{\star}\neq 0 . (With exact queries, Hopkins et al. (2020b) use O ⁡ ( n ​ log 2 ​ n ​ log ⁡ ( N / δ ′ ) ) O(n\log^{2}n\log(N/\delta^{\prime})) .)

sections.text: Theorem 3.7 bounds labels uniformly. Its unlabeled cost can still be quantified in terms of the angular cap-mass function. In the language of splitting indices ( Dasgupta, 2005 , Hanneke, 2014 ) , a splitter is a query that separates many pairs of candidate hypotheses. The function a μ a_{\mu} measures the availability of approximate splitters under the unlabeled distribution, while point location determines their informativeness . Theorem 3.10 (Pathwise unlabeled cost) . Answer the queries from a dedicated independent stream of unlabeled examples, and let point location use only accepted points and labels, not rejected draws or waiting lengths. sections.heading: 4 When the angular assumptions or a finite pool are not enough
sections.text: The positive theorem uses two angular assumptions for two different reasons. Hyperplane-nullness gives anti-concentration near every great subsphere, and symmetric full support places points near every desired query direction or its antipode. Section 4.1 shows that each is necessary for a general equivalence, even with unlimited unlabeled data. Neither is necessary for every individual distribution. Many marginals with smaller angular support, or with hyperplane mass, remain easy. Section 4.2 then shows that even with both assumptions, the amount of unlabeled data can be forced to be arbitrarily large.

sections.heading: 4.1 Necessity of the angular assumptions
sections.text: Both constructions place mass near the points p i = ( t i , t i 2 , 1 ) p_{i}=(t_{i},t_{i}^{2},1) , t i = i / ( m + 1 ) t_{i}=i/(m+1) , on the moment curve t ↦ ( t , t 2 , 1 ) t\mapsto(t,t^{2},1) . For each i i some homogeneous halfspace labels p i p_{i} negative and every other p j p_{j} positive, so each p i p_{i} can only be informative about its own alternative target, while membership queries off the support can binary-search over i i . Proofs are in Section C.1 , and Table 3 summarizes the role of each assumption. Proposition 4.1 (Symmetric full support is necessary) . For every m ≥ 2 m\geq 2 there are a distribution D m D_{m} on ℝ 3 \mathbb{R}^{3} and m + 1 m+1 homogeneous halfspaces such that, at accuracy ε = 1 / ( 4 ​ m ) \varepsilon=1/(4m) and success probability 3 / 4 3/4 : (i) every pool learner needs at least m / 2 m/2 labels in the worst case, even with unlimited unlabeled examples, knowledge of D m D_{m} , and improper output, (ii) a membership-query learner identifies the target exactly with at most 1 + ⌈ log 2 ⁡ m ⌉ 1+\lceil\log_{2}m\rceil labels. Moreover D m D_{m} may be taken to have a smooth density (hence a hyperplane-null angular law), and to be centrally symmetric. Only symmetric full support fails. Proposition 4.1 is the distributional form of the classical one-point-per-target obstruction ( Dasgupta, 2004 ) . It shows that hyperplane-nullness does not suffice even with a smooth, symmetric density. Proposition 4.2 (Hyperplane-nullness is necessary) . For every m ≥ 2 m\geq 2 there are a full-support distribution D m D_{m} on ℝ 4 \mathbb{R}^{4} and an infinite family of homogeneous halfspaces, containing arbitrarily small tilts of one target, such that, for ε = 1 / ( 16 ​ m ) \varepsilon=1/(16m) : (i) membership queries achieve error at most ε \varepsilon using 1 + ⌈ log 2 ⁡ m ⌉ 1+\lceil\log_{2}m\rceil labels, (ii) any pool learner that terminates almost surely and succeeds with probability at least 3 / 4 3/4 for every target uses at least m / 2 m/2 labels in expectation on some target, even with unlimited unlabeled data. The construction places mass on the target hyperplane and uses arbitrarily small tilts ( Remark C.1 ). Hyperplane-nullness excludes such mass, and this is what makes a target-independent margin floor possible.

sections.heading: Lifted affine problems.
sections.text: Lifting an affine halfspace in ℝ n − 1 \mathbb{R}^{n-1} via x ↦ ( x , 1 ) x\mapsto(x,1) makes it homogeneous and confines all directions to an open hemisphere. Since h w ​ ( − x ) = − h w ​ ( x ) h_{w}(-x)=-h_{w}(x) whenever ⟨ w , x ⟩ ≠ 0 \langle w,x\rangle\neq 0 , only the symmetrized angular law matters, and for a lifted marginal it has full support exactly when the original marginal has full support on ℝ n − 1 \mathbb{R}^{n-1} ( Corollary 3.9 ). Marginals with bounded or otherwise incomplete support, such as the uniform ball, leave some neighborhood of the equator uncharged. Proposition 4.1 is an explicit instance, and Theorem 4.5 below shows that the same obstruction can reappear inside a high-probability core of a full-support law when the unlabeled budget is bounded.

sections.heading: 4.2 Finite unlabeled budgets

Above it, a Grünbaum-type inequality bounds the Tukey depth of the mean below, uniformly over the class ( Theorem D.14 ). The threshold − 1 / n -1/n is intrinsic to the angular geometry. Together with Proposition D.32 this gives the exact worst-case disagreement exponent ( n − 2 ) / n (n-2)/n , and Corollaries G.1 and G.2 give the matching label exponent under an unlabeled budget fixed in advance, up to logarithms. The proof first treats uniform convex bodies by a projective change of variables and then integrates over the level sets of f f . Projecting f f itself would lose too much concavity near s = − 1 / n s=-1/n .

sections.heading: 6 Application to annotation and certification of learned verifiers
sections.text: A generator produces unlabeled reasoning states, while expert judgments of their validity are expensive labels. Let ϕ ⁡ ( Z ) ∈ ℝ n ∖ { 0 } \phi(Z)\in\mathbb{R}^{n}\setminus\{0\} be a fixed known representation and let h ⋆ ​ ( Z ) = sign ⁡ ⟨ w ⋆ , ϕ ⁡ ( Z ) ⟩ h^{\star}(Z)=\operatorname{sign}\langle w^{\star},\phi(Z)\rangle be realizable. The angular assumptions concern which feature directions the generator produces, and Section E.1 discusses the scope of this modeling choice. Theorem 3.7 applies to offline annotation, in which the learner selects which generated states to label. Coupling the learned and perfect-verifier executions until their first different verdict transfers error under the exploration law to deployment. If the laws of the states visited by the perfect verifier have densities at most C t C_{t} relative to the exploration law, then for every ξ ∈ ( 0 , 1 ) \xi\in(0,1) , O ⁡ ( n ​ log 3 ​ n ​ log ⁡ ( n ​ ∑ t C t / ( ξ ​ δ ) ) ) O(n\log^{3}n\log(n\sum_{t}C_{t}/(\xi\delta))) labels give agreement of the whole deployment trajectory with probability 1 − δ − ξ 1-\delta-\xi ( Corollary E.2 ). Theorem E.1 extends this to unbounded density ratios through a coverage profile, and Proposition E.4 replaces coverage of full state laws by angular occupancy. Theorem 3.8 separates the assumptions on evaluation and annotation. Evaluation directions must be hyperplane-null, whereas the law of proposed states, which plays the role of the query law of Theorem 3.8 and which we call the proposal law , only needs symmetric full support and may be atomic ( Section E.4 ). A supplied positive margin permits exact certification of a known finite deployment set using O ⁡ ( n ​ log 3 ​ n ​ log ⁡ ( M / δ ) ) O(n\log^{3}n\log(M/\delta)) labels, and directional nets extend certification to infinite sets ( Section E.5 ). Bounds on the number of proposals and a zero-margin obstruction make the access requirements explicit ( Section E.6 ). Theorem E.13 compares three training interfaces on one two-dimensional family with M = 2 m M=2^{m} targets. At fixed confidence, successful-trace behavioral cloning needs Θ ⁡ ( M ) \Theta(M) demonstrations. Active annotation uses m m expert verdicts but needs Ω ⁡ ( M ) \Omega(M) pool states. Interaction uses m m states and m m verdicts. The objective is to learn the verdicts, or to reproduce the perfect-verifier trajectory, rather than to succeed at a task by imitation. Proofs and interface definitions are in Appendix E .

sections.heading: 7 Related work
sections.text: Our contribution is a target-independent, robust simulation of synthesized queries from ordinary sample access, together with quantitative accessibility bounds and sharp separations between the label complexity, which is uniform over marginals, and the number of unlabeled examples, which is not. Separately, we give the sharp s s -concave phase diagram, including a matching intermediate exponent. We group prior work by the part of this contribution it bears on.

sections.heading: Pool access, membership queries, and point location.
sections.text: Point location in hyperplane arrangements ( Meiser, 1993 , Ezra and Sharir, 2019 , Ezra et al., 2020 ) labels a finite set of N N points with a number of linear queries polynomial in n n and logarithmic in N N , and Hopkins et al. (2020b) give a near-optimal active-learning form that uses O ~ ​ ( n ​ log ⁡ N ) \tilde{O}(n\log N) synthesized queries. We do not give a new exact-query point-location theorem. We make the algorithm of Hopkins et al. (2020b) tolerate subspace-relative query uncertainty and show that an ordinary pool provides such an oracle with a target-independent precision. Wang and Dughmi (2026) ask which classes are easy under synthesis, through adaptive identification complexity and the synthesized halving dimension. We ask when a marginal makes the needed queries accessible to a pool, where exact-query guarantees do not survive because a nearby pool point may lie across the boundary. Without synthesis, Black et al. (2026) show that on an arbitrary finite point set, restricting the normal to K K known directions gives query complexity governed by K + log ⁡ N K+\log N , and Propositions 4.1 and 4.2 are distributional versions of the classical obstruction. Diakonikolas et al. (2024) prove an information-theoretic lower bound for affine halfspaces under 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , I ) \mathcal{N}(0,I) . For a random halfspace of bias b b , any pool learner with m ≥ poly ⁡ ( d / b ) m\geq\mathrm{poly}(d/b) unlabeled examples needs Ω ~ ​ ( d / ( b ​ log ⁡ m ) ) \tilde{\Omega}(d/(b\log m)) labels to reach error b / 2 b/2 . So reaching that error with k k labels requires log ⁡ m = Ω ~ ​ ( d / ( b ​ k ) ) \log m=\tilde{\Omega}(d/(bk)) , and in particular polylogarithmically many labels require a pool of size exp ⁡ ( Ω ~ ​ ( d / b ) ) \exp(\tilde{\Omega}(d/b)) . Membership queries, in contrast, give efficient agnostic learning with O ~ ​ ( min ⁡ { 1 / b , 1 / ε } + d ​ polylog ​ ( 1 / ε ) ) \tilde{O}(\min\{1/b,1/\varepsilon\}+d\,\mathrm{polylog}(1/\varepsilon)) queries. They remark that pools approach membership queries as they grow exponentially. Corollary 3.9 makes this precise in labels for general halfspaces under every full-support marginal with no mass on affine hyperplanes, including 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , I ) \mathcal{N}(0,I) . With an unlimited pool, O ⁡ ( d ​ log 3 ​ d ​ log ⁡ ( d / ( ε ​ δ ) ) ) O(d\log^{3}d\log(d/(\varepsilon\delta))) labels suffice. Their lower bound then forces any learner with this label count to inspect exp ⁡ ( Ω ~ ​ ( 1 / ε ) ) \exp(\tilde{\Omega}(1/\varepsilon)) unlabeled examples on their instances. Other relaxed query models differ from ours in what an answer means. Comparison queries ( Hopkins et al., 2020c , Hopkins et al., 2020a , Kane et al., 2017 , Kane et al., 2018 ) return relative information, not a label at a nearby point. Unreliable boundary queries ( Blum et al., 1995 ) allow wrong or “don’t know” answers near the boundary under a marginal with no mass there, and yield polynomial-time learners for intersections of two halfspaces, extending Baum (1990) , and for subclasses of monotone DNF. Our subspace-relative oracle with a margin floor is a relative, data-driven analogue aimed at near-optimal query complexity. Awasthi et al. (2013) restrict synthesized queries to neighborhoods of random examples, whereas our locality is angular and every label is that of an actual sample. Gonen et al. (2013) analyze a margin-based pool algorithm, but a margin-dependent bound with a possibly tiny floor does not give a uniform label rate.

sections.heading: Disagreement, splitting, and star-based lower bounds.
sections.text: CAL ( Cohn et al., 1994 ) queries exactly where the version space disagrees, and the disagreement coefficient ( Hanneke, 2007 , Hanneke, 2014 ) bounds how often. It is the route from our s s -concave disagreement bounds to label bounds. The simulation theorem needs no small disagreement coefficient, and a large disagreement region is not by itself a lower bound for every learner, which is why our lower bounds are proved directly ( Lemma A.3 ). Dasgupta’s splitting index ( Dasgupta, 2005 ) (see also Hanneke, 2014 , Sec. 8.2 ) separates informativeness , how many hypothesis pairs a query splits, from availability , the probability τ \tau (in his notation) that the unlabeled distribution produces such a query. In our setting availability is the cap mass a μ ¯ a_{\bar{\mu}} of the symmetrized angular law, and Q Q adaptive queries at radius γ \gamma cost O ⁡ ( Q ​ a μ ¯ ​ ( γ ) − 1 ​ log ⁡ ( Q / δ ) ) O(Q\,a_{\bar{\mu}}(\gamma)^{-1}\log(Q/\delta)) draws with high probability. The guarantees differ in two ways. Dasgupta’s upper bound for a ( ρ , ε , τ ) (\rho,\varepsilon,\tau) -splittable class uses O ~ ​ ( n / ρ ) \tilde{O}(n/\rho) labels whose hidden logarithmic factors include log ⁡ ( 1 / τ ) \log(1/\tau) , which depends on the marginal, whereas Theorem 3.7 has no marginal-dependent factor. And his splittability guarantee for halfspaces ( Dasgupta, 2005 , Theorem 5) is local and for the uniform sphere, whereas we need no splitting guarantee for an arbitrary angular law. Hanneke and Yang (2015) give distribution-free minimax bounds governed by the star number, which is infinite for halfspaces and gives Ω ⁡ ( 1 / ε ) \Omega(1/\varepsilon) over unrestricted marginals. Wiener et al. (2015) refine disagreement-based analyses through version-space compression, and Hanneke (2024) relates the star number to the VC dimension of version spaces and disagreement regions. Our lower bounds are star configurations whose cap masses are chosen to match the accuracy and the unlabeled budget.

sections.heading: Distribution-specific halfspaces and the s s -concave phase diagram.
sections.text: Margin localization ( Balcan and Long, 2013 , Awasthi et al., 2017 , Balcan and Zhang, 2017 ) queries labels in a shrinking band around the current estimate and gives efficient learners under log-concave and s s -concave laws, also with Massart and Tsybakov noise ( Zhang and Li, 2021 , Li and Zhang, 2024 ) . These results give noise tolerance, polynomial unlabeled cost and polynomial runtime under stronger geometry. Their analysis needs band masses, disagreement outside the band and conditional moments, the inputs Balcan and Zhang (2017) develop for s s -concave laws via Bobkov’s heavy-tail concentration ( Bobkov, 2007 ) . Our margin floor has a different role. It sets the accuracy at which a sampled direction can stand in for a synthesized query. For the phase diagram we use known radial-body and concavity results: Ball’s bodies ( Ball, 1988 ) and Bobkov’s extension ( Bobkov, 2010 ) , moment and centroid estimates ( Adamczak et al., 2012 , Fradelizi et al., 2020 , Marsiglietti and Pandey, 2021 ) , the Fradelizi–Guédon–Pajor comparisons ( Fradelizi et al., 2014 ) , the entropy and convexity facts surveyed by Madiman et al. (2017) , and the Bárány–Larman bound on the small-mass halfspace region of a convex body ( Bárány and Larman, 1988 ) . Our new ingredients are the projective and level-set argument of Section 5.1 , which gives the sharp intermediate exponent ( n − 2 ) / n (n-2)/n , and the positive-depth refinement ( Proposition G.3 ), which shows that logarithmic disagreement holds for all s > − 1 / n s>-1/n at reference points of uniformly positive depth. The results of Bárány et al. (2020) on these regions for general measures do not give the concavity-dependent bound. Symmetry gives depth 1 / 2 1/2 , which is why the symmetric and general thresholds differ.

sections.heading: Quantifier order.
sections.text: Balcan et al. (2010) separate achieving small error from certifying it, and activization ( Hanneke, 2012 ) improves asymptotic label complexity on fixed problems. Our bound is instead uniform over all targets and all admissible marginals, and only the number of unlabeled examples depends on the marginal. The two recent frameworks closest in spirit use different quantifiers ( Table 1 ). Hanneke et al. (2024) fix the unlabeled budget before execution and let rate constants depend on the distribution, so our lower bounds, whose hard distribution varies with the budget and accuracy, do not bound a universal rate for one fixed distribution. Hanneke et al. (2025b) require uniformity over targets for a fixed marginal but concern passive sample size. Two reductions make the comparison concrete. If our algorithm uses N U N_{U} unlabeled examples and otherwise fails with probability at most δ \delta , stopping it after u u examples gives 𝔼 ⁡ [ err ] ≤ ε + δ + Pr ⁡ ( N U > u ) , \mathbb{E}[\operatorname{err}]\leq\varepsilon+\delta+\Pr(N_{U}>u), so an algorithm in the framework of Hanneke et al. (2024) needs a choice of u u that does not depend on the distribution, and almost-sure finiteness of N U N_{U} does not provide one. Conversely, simulating a pool algorithm on u u fully labeled examples costs u u passive labels, so active label savings do not become passive sample savings. Partial concept classes ( Alon et al., 2021 ) are the natural formalism for the admissible queries of Section E.1 , and Hanneke et al. sections.heading: Noise and verifier supervision.
sections.text: General agnostic active learners ( Balcan et al., 2009 , Dasgupta et al., 2007 ) , importance weighting ( Beygelzimer et al., 2009 ) , analyses beyond disagreement ( Zhang and Chaudhuri, 2014 ) , and experimental design over a pool ( Katz-Samuels et al., 2021 ) address noise rather than access. Hanneke (2025) removes disagreement penalties from the leading agnostic term, with bound O ⁡ ( OPT 2 ε 2 ​ ( d + log ⁡ 1 δ ) ) + O ~ ​ ( d / ε ) O\bigl(\tfrac{\mathrm{OPT}^{2}}{\varepsilon^{2}}(d+\log\tfrac{1}{\delta})\bigr)+\tilde{O}(d/\varepsilon) , where OPT \mathrm{OPT} is the error of the best classifier in the class. The residual d / ε d/\varepsilon term means it does not give our realizable polylogarithmic rate. Related models for verifiers include reliable apprenticeship ( Hanneke et al., 2025a ) and online selective sampling ( Hanneke and Yang, 2021 ) . Robustly-reliable learners output, with each prediction, a level of training-data poisoning up to which the prediction is guaranteed to be correct, also in active learning ( Balcan et al., 2022 ) , and Balcan et al. (2023) give such guarantees under test-time attacks and distribution shift. Blum et al. (2025) study short certificates for reliable predictions. Balcan et al. (2025) develop PAC objectives for learned chain-of-thought verifiers, and Balcan et al. (2026) analyze online verifier learning under generator–verifier feedback. We impose the coverage assumption in advance and do not show that feedback-induced shift satisfies it.

sections.heading: 8 Discussion and open problems
sections.text: Under two qualitative angular assumptions, each necessary, a pool learner matches the membership-query label rate uniformly over marginals and targets. The number of unlabeled examples depends on the marginal, and the lower bounds show that this dependence cannot be removed. The results therefore describe a tradeoff between labels and unlabeled examples, in the spirit of the splitting-index distinction between informativeness and availability, rather than an equivalence between the two query models. For s s -concave marginals the thresholds are sharp, and so are the polynomial rates below them.

sections.heading: The label–unlabeled tradeoff for a fixed angular law.
sections.text: Characterize the achievable pairs (unlabeled samples, labels) for a fixed angular law μ \mu , interpolating between unlimited unlabeled access ( Theorem 3.7 ) and a distribution-uniform budget ( Propositions 4.3 and 4.5 ). Our upper bound depends on μ \mu through the cap masses a μ ¯ ​ ( γ j ) a_{\bar{\mu}}(\gamma_{j}) and on the conditioning κ ⁡ ( T j ) \kappa(T_{j}) of the data-dependent isotropic transforms ( Theorem 3.10 ). How do cap accessibility and transform conditioning enter the optimal tradeoff? A concrete first step is to bound κ ⁡ ( T j ) \kappa(T_{j}) , with high probability over the passive sample, by a function of n n , N N , and a general-position parameter of the sample such as σ gp = min | S | = n ⁡ σ min ​ ( Y S ) \sigma_{\mathrm{gp}}=\min_{|S|=n}\sigma_{\min}(Y_{S}) from Lemma C.2 . Such a bound would turn Theorem 3.10 into a high-probability unlabeled bound in terms of a μ ¯ a_{\bar{\mu}} and the small-ball probabilities of μ \mu . Bounding the expected cost would further require integrability, for example control of 𝔼 ⁡ [ 1 / a μ ¯ ​ ( γ j ) ] \mathbb{E}[1/a_{\bar{\mu}}(\gamma_{j})] . An almost surely finite cost can have infinite expectation.

sections.heading: Fixed-distribution rates.
sections.text: Let k k be the label budget and u ⁡ ( k ) u(k) an unlabeled schedule that the learner fixes before seeing data. Our lower bounds let the marginal depend on the accuracy and on the schedule. Two fixed-distribution questions remain. First, for one fixed marginal D D satisfying our assumptions and worst-case targets, is there a polynomial schedule u ⁡ ( k ) u(k) under which the optimal error decays only polynomially in k k , although it decays as exp ⁡ ( − Ω ⁡ ( k / ( n ​ log 3 ​ n ) ) ) \exp(-\Omega(k/(n\log^{3}n))) with unlimited unlabeled data? Second, the same question for the universal rates of Hanneke et al. (2024) , in which D D and the target are both fixed and the rate constants may depend on them.

sections.heading: An efficient margin floor with a quality guarantee.
sections.text: The explicit floor costs M 0 O ⁡ ( n ) M_{0}^{O(n)} arithmetic operations ( Section C.2 ). A positive floor alone is not enough, since an overly conservative floor makes the cap-waiting cost prohibitive. In the arithmetic model on a sample of size M 0 M_{0} , is there an algorithm running in time polynomial in n n and M 0 M_{0} that outputs an admissible floor within a factor poly ⁡ ( n ) \mathrm{poly}(n) of the largest width whose worst empirical band mass is at most δ / ( 32 ​ N ) \delta/(32N) ?

sections.heading: Joint geometry of disagreement.
sections.text: Theorem 5.2 gives the uniform bound θ D ( ε ) ≤ C n ( 1 + n s ) − 1 ε − ( n − 2 ) / n \theta_{D}(\varepsilon)\leq C_{n}(1+ns)^{-1}\varepsilon^{-(n-2)/n} for − 1 / n < s ≤ − 1 / ( n + 1 ) -1/n<s\leq-1/(n+1) , and Proposition G.3 gives O ⁡ ( log ⁡ ( 1 / ε ) ) O(\log(1/\varepsilon)) at reference points of positive depth. What is the optimal joint dependence of the disagreement coefficient on the accuracy, the depth of the reference point, the dimension, and 1 + n ​ s 1+ns ? Matching logarithmic lower bounds in the regimes where we prove O ⁡ ( log ⁡ ( 1 / ε ) ) O(\log(1/\varepsilon)) are also open, and more broadly one may ask which angular geometries between elliptical and arbitrary centrally symmetric laws have logarithmic disagreement.

sections.heading: Adversarial noise and agents.
sections.text: Under Massart noise the pool simulation extends by majority votes ( Corollary F.2 ). Adversarial noise can concentrate on the rare caps that the simulation uses, so an analogue of Theorem 3.7 needs point location that tolerates both relative query uncertainty and adversarially placed label errors. A related direction is to study active learning when the examples are agents who can improve their features in response to the deployed classifier ( Attias et al., 2025 , Sharma and Sun, 2025 ) .

sections.heading: Data-driven active learning.
sections.text: Our learners set their parameters, such as the margin floor, the tolerance η \eta , the cap precision γ \gamma and the unlabeled schedule, by worst-case analysis. Data-driven algorithm design ( Balcan, 2020 ) instead tunes such parameters on a sample of related tasks, with generalization guarantees for the tuned choice. For learning with few labels, this approach has mainly been developed for semi-supervised learning (also pool-based, but the learner cannot decide which points to label) where the similarity graph and the hyperparameters are learned across tasks ( Balcan and Sharma, 2021 , Sharma and Jones, 2023 , Du et al., 2025 ) . Our work motivates data-driven configuration of active learning algorithms. Propositions 4.3 and 4.5 rule out an unlabeled budget that works uniformly over marginals, but they leave open whether a budget, margin floor or query rule tuned on tasks from an unknown task distribution can achieve near-optimal label and unlabeled costs on average over that distribution.

sections.heading: Secondary directions.
sections.text: Robust point location costs one extra log ⁡ n \log n factor over the exact-query learner, and removing it would require a selection rule with the comparison cost of exact median selection under an imprecise comparator ( Appendix B ). For verifiers, the central question is whether interactive pools can match the label rate of Theorem 3.7 under feedback-induced state shift, without the coverage assumption (see also Section E.7 ).

sections.text: Lemma C.2 (Explicit empirical floor) . Let Y 1 , … , Y M 0 ∈ S n − 1 Y_{1},\dots,Y_{M_{0}}\in S^{n-1} be i.i.d. from a hyperplane-null angular law. For S ⊆ [ M 0 ] S\subseteq[M_{0}] with | S | = n |S|=n , let Y S Y_{S} be the n × n n\times n matrix with rows Y i ⊤ Y_{i}^{\top} , i ∈ S i\in S , and define θ alg = 1 2 ​ n ​ min | S | = n ​ σ min ​ ( Y S ) \theta_{\mathrm{alg}}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{n}}\min_{|S|=n}\sigma_{\min}(Y_{S}) . Then θ alg > 0 \theta_{\mathrm{alg}}>0 almost surely and no band of width θ alg \theta_{\mathrm{alg}} contains n n sample points, so every such band has empirical mass at most ( n − 1 ) / M 0 (n-1)/M_{0} . With the sample size M 0 M_{0} of Lemma 3.2 , the same relative VC bound gives ρ μ ​ ( θ alg ) ≤ δ / ( 8 ​ N ) \rho_{\mu}(\theta_{\mathrm{alg}})\leq\delta/(8N) with probability at least 1 − δ / 8 1-\delta/8 . Proof. Hyperplane-nullness implies every fixed n n -tuple is linearly independent almost surely. A finite union makes this simultaneous over all subsets. If a band contained the n n points indexed by S S , then for its unit normal w w , ‖ Y S ​ w ‖ 2 < n ​ θ alg ≤ 1 2 ​ σ min ​ ( Y S ) \|Y_{S}w\|_{2}<\sqrt{n}\,\theta_{\mathrm{alg}}\leq\frac{1}{2}\sigma_{\min}(Y_{S}) , contradicting ‖ Y S ​ w ‖ 2 ≥ σ min ​ ( Y S ) \|Y_{S}w\|_{2}\geq\sigma_{\min}(Y_{S}) . The empirical and population bounds follow from the same relative-deviation estimate as in Lemma 3.2 . ∎ The direct implementation enumerates ( M 0 n ) \binom{M_{0}}{n} subsets and costs M 0 O ⁡ ( n ) M_{0}^{O(n)} arithmetic operations. Theorem 3.7 is a statement about labels and unlabeled examples, and we make no running-time claim for it. Apart from the floor, the queries and tests of Appendix B use only linear algebra on the current sample. The remaining step is to find the dense subspace and approximate isotropic transform of Hopkins et al. (2020b, Cor. 4.20) , whose existence is all that Hopkins et al. (2020b) need, since they measure query depth. Algorithms for approximate Forster and radial-isotropic transforms exist ( Hardt and Moitra, 2013 , Diakonikolas et al., 2023 ) , but we have not verified that they cover the weighted subspace search, the precision, and the boosted distributions required here. The explicit floor is dimension-exponential, and the cap-waiting cost in Theorem 3.10 can be arbitrarily large. Propositions 4.3 and 4.5 show that no distribution-independent algorithmic optimization can remove the latter dependence.

sections.heading: Appendix D Proofs for s s -concave marginals
sections.text: This appendix proves the results summarized in Section 5 . Balcan and Zhang (2017) developed their tools and sample-based active learners for − 1 / ( 2 n + 3 ) ≤ s ≤ 0 -1/(2n+3)\leq s\leq 0 . Several of the underlying geometric and moment facts are classical. This appendix applies known convex geometry to wider ranges of s s , gives the matching sharpness examples, and constructs the symmetric endpoint example of Section D.6 . Throughout, χ = − 1 / s − ( n + 2 ) \chi=-1/s-(n+2) is the slack of Section 5 .

sections.text: Let Λ ∗ ​ ( ε , δ , 𝒟 n , s ) \Lambda^{*}(\varepsilon,\delta;\mathcal{D}_{n,s}) denote the minimax number of labels that a pool learner with unlimited unlabeled data needs to reach error ε \varepsilon with probability at least 1 − δ 1-\delta , uniformly over D ∈ 𝒟 n , s D\in\mathcal{D}_{n,s} and homogeneous targets. Corollary D.3 (All finite s s ) . For every n ≥ 2 n\geq 2 and every finite s ≤ 0 s\leq 0 , c ⁡ ( n − 1 ) ​ log ⁡ ( 1 / ε ) ≤ Λ ∗ ​ ( ε , δ , 𝒟 n , s ) ≤ C ​ n ​ log 3 ​ n ​ log ​ n ε ​ δ c(n-1)\log(1/\varepsilon)\leq\Lambda^{*}(\varepsilon,\delta;\mathcal{D}_{n,s})\leq Cn\log^{3}n\log\frac{n}{\varepsilon\delta} for constant confidence. In particular, with unlimited unlabeled data the minimax label complexity is Θ ⁡ ( n ​ log ⁡ ( 1 / ε ) ) \Theta(n\log(1/\varepsilon)) up to a log 3 ⁡ n \log^{3}n factor (and logarithmic confidence terms), for every finite s s . Proof. A full-dimensional s s -concave law has convex support and its mean lies in the interior. The density is positive and continuous on a neighborhood of the mean. After centering at the mean, the angular law is therefore absolutely continuous with respect to spherical measure and every open cap receives positive probability. The upper bound follows from Theorem 3.7 . For the lower bound, take the uniform distribution on a Euclidean ball, which is s s -concave for every s ≤ 0 s\leq 0 . Angular disagreement is proportional to the angle between target normals, so a spherical packing and the information bound of Kulkarni et al. (1993) give Ω ⁡ ( ( n − 1 ) ​ log ⁡ ( 1 / ε ) ) \Omega((n-1)\log(1/\varepsilon)) labels. ∎

sections.heading: Appendix E Learned verifiers, modeling and proofs
sections.text: The pool theorem also applies when labels are expert judgments of generated reasoning states. Generation provides cheap exploration, annotation provides expensive validity judgments, and deployment requires repeated verifier decisions along an adaptive trajectory. This application assumes a realizable linear representation and exploration laws that satisfy the hypotheses of Theorem 3.7 or of its two-law form, Theorem 3.8 .

sections.heading: Scope of the model.
sections.text: First, an affine verifier sign ⁡ ( ⟨ w , ϕ ⁡ ( Z ) ⟩ + b ) \operatorname{sign}(\langle w,\phi(Z)\rangle+b) can be made homogeneous by appending a constant coordinate. The augmented directions lie in one hemisphere, but only the symmetrized angular law matters, and symmetric full support holds exactly when the feature law has full support in ℝ n \mathbb{R}^{n} ( Corollary 3.9 ). It fails for bounded feature maps, whose lifted directions avoid a neighborhood of the equator ( Section 4.1 ). Second, for n ≥ 2 n\geq 2 a deterministic embedding of finite token strings induces an atomic law on a countable set, and every atom lies on some hyperplane through the origin, so it cannot be hyperplane-null. This matters only for the law under which error is measured. Theorem 3.8 allows an atomic proposal law as long as the evaluation directions are hyperplane-null ( Section E.4 ). Continuous randomization of the representation could remove atoms, but would require a separate argument that it preserves labels and provides the required support. The results of this appendix are therefore a geometric model of when selective annotation can replace synthesized queries. They make no claim about arbitrary tokenized prompts or language-model embeddings.

sections.heading: Pools versus membership queries.
sections.text: An arbitrary synthesized input may be malformed, ambiguous, outside the expert’s competence, or too expensive to assess. An invalid proposed step can usually still be labeled “incorrect,” and an unsolvable problem can be labeled if the task allows that answer. The actual obstacle is that a reliable, affordable labeling oracle may exist only on an admissible subset of inputs. A natural formalization is a partial concept c ⋆ : 𝒵 → { − 1 , + 1 , ⊥ } , A ⋆ = { z : c ⋆ ( z ) ≠ ⊥ } , c^{\star}:\mathcal{Z}\to\{-1,+1,\bot\},\qquad A^{\star}=\{z:c^{\star}(z)\neq\bot\}, where ⊥ \bot means the annotation task is undefined or unavailable. If the exploration law satisfies ν ⁡ ( A ⋆ ) = 1 \nu(A^{\star})=1 , pool queries are always admissible, while an unrestricted membership-query learner may query outside A ⋆ A^{\star} . Allowing it to receive ⊥ \bot gives a different oracle model, connected to partial concept classes ( Alon et al., 2021 ) , which our halfspace results do not analyze. Synthesized vectors in embedding space may also correspond to no reasoning state at all, and a candidate following an invalid prefix needs a precisely specified judgment (local inference validity, valid-prefix status, or extendability to a correct solution). Membership queries remain meaningful as a stronger comparison model that allows expert judgments on specified counterfactual continuations. This does not grant access to labels of arbitrary feature vectors.

sections.heading: Three access models.
sections.text: Table 7 distinguishes selecting labels from controlling which states are available. Model What it provides Limitation under feedback-induced shift Fixed offline pool Selective annotation of previously generated states Cannot acquire states absent from exploration Interactive pool Fresh candidates generated at learner-induced prefixes, then selectively annotated Requires exploration and supervision on the evolving state distribution Membership queries Labels of constructed admissible prefix–candidate pairs Useful only if such states can be constructed and reliably labeled Table 7: Access models for verifier supervision. Interactive pool-based learning is a natural model for chain-of-thought verification. At a current prefix, generate several candidate continuations, inspect them cheaply, and request expert judgments on selected candidates. The verifier’s decisions determine future prefixes, so the pool changes during training. We establish two kinds of guarantees. Offline replacement ( Sections E.3 and E.5 ). Coverage of the perfect-verifier path, or a known deployment set with a supplied positive margin, suffices for high-probability agreement of the whole deployment trajectory, because before the first different verdict both executions share their history. This avoids coverage after an error but does not guarantee recovery after divergence. Interaction versus pools ( Section E.7 ). Adaptive state generation can replace a large offline pool. Applying Theorem 3.7 to successive interactive pools would require additional conditional-support, sampling, confidence and deployment analysis that we do not provide. This leaves open how much expert supervision and state exploration are needed when the verifier both selects labels and influences future examples.

sections.heading: E.2 Exploration and annotation
sections.text: We identify states with their representations. The exploration law ν \nu produces i.i.d. unlabeled states that can be inspected before annotation. Its angular law is hyperplane-null with symmetric full support about the verifier’s origin. Section E.4 separates these two roles. A noiseless expert returns h ⋆ ​ ( z ) h^{\star}(z) . Passive annotation labels naturally occurring states. Offline active annotation adaptively selects labels from an exploration pool. Interactive annotation additionally changes which states become available. Each labeled state counts as one annotation. If an expert call reveals a trajectory, its information and cost must be accounted for separately.

sections.heading: Verifier classes.
sections.text: The results cover realizable linear probes on frozen features and linear combinations of fixed verifier scores, but not arbitrary neural verifiers or jointly learned representations. Affine rules are covered by lifting, as discussed in Section E.1 . The learning reductions also apply outside verification, and the execution coupling and the proposal interface connect them to verdict-dependent generation.

sections.heading: E.7 Separating demonstrations, active annotation, and interaction
sections.text:
We distinguish three training interfaces. In successful-trace behavioral cloning (BC), the learner receives independent expert demonstrations but cannot choose their states or ask for counterfactual verdicts. Our examples use one-step successful traces, so each demonstration consists of one accepted state. The learner may process these demonstrations arbitrarily. The lower bounds do not restrict the fitting algorithm. In offline active annotation , the learner inspects an i.i.d. unlabeled pool from a specified target-independent law and adaptively requests verdicts only on its elements. In interactive verification , a known generator can change its next proposal using previous expert verdicts. It has no access to the unknown target except through those verdicts. Every generated state and expert verdict is counted separately. Deployment receives no expert feedback. The common objective below is to learn the expert’s verdict function, or reproduce its verdict trajectory. This is stronger than merely producing some valid answer. In particular, a BC lower bound for this objective is not a lower bound on every possible task-success objective for an imitation policy. Theorem E.13 (A three-way separation in two dimensions) . sections.heading: Interpretation.
sections.text: At fixed confidence, Table 8 separates two resources exponentially in m = log 2 ⁡ M m=\log_{2}M . Active annotation saves supervision relative to successful traces, and interaction saves state acquisition relative to offline annotation. The offline pool bounds differ by a logarithm, and because adjacent targets differ in population by only 1 / ( 2 ​ M ) 1/(2M) , the offline lower bound concerns deployment-sensitive coverage. The difference lies in the interface. A fixed pool contains only states generated in advance, whereas DAgger ( Ross et al., 2011 ) and the offline datasets of Balcan et al. (2026, Remark 2.15) can supply labels on learner-induced or adaptively generated prefixes, a stronger form of access. Proposition E.14 (Successful traces need not identify counterfactual verdicts) . There is a two-element class of homogeneous verifiers in ℝ 2 \mathbb{R}^{2} and an expert demonstration policy producing identical successful traces under both targets, such that any learner using only those traces has worst-target error at least 1 / 2 1/2 on one specified deployment verdict. Active annotation from a uniform-circle pool identifies the target with one expert verdict and finite expected generation cost. Controlled interaction does so with one state and one verdict. Proof. Take w + = ( 1 , 1 ) / 2 w_{+}=(1,1)/\sqrt{2} and w − = ( − 1 , 1 ) / 2 w_{-}=(-1,1)/\sqrt{2} . The demonstration policy always returns the valid one-step trace with feature e 2 e_{2} , positive under both targets. Deployment asks for the verdict at e 1 e_{1} , whose labels are opposite. Identical training laws force average failure at least 1 / 2 1/2 under the equal target prior, even with arbitrarily many demonstrations. The two targets disagree on half of the circle, so an active annotator can wait for that known region and identify the target from one label. The expected wait is two samples. An interactive generator can propose e 1 e_{1} directly. ∎ This example isolates absent coverage in the demonstration policy. It does not imply that copying the demonstrated action fails to produce a valid answer. That action is valid for both targets. The separation concerns learning a verifier for counterfactual proposals. By contrast, Theorem E.13 uses nondegenerate, target-dependent demonstrations covering every accepted direction.

sections.heading: Open questions.
sections.text: Beyond the interactive question raised in Section 8 , two problems are concrete. First, can a reachable deployment set be certified when it is only implicit, generated by the deployment system rather than enumerated as in Theorem E.7 ? Second, can the supplied margin be replaced by adaptation to an unknown positive deployment margin? Proposition E.12 shows that some positive margin is necessary.

sections.heading: Appendix F Noise
sections.text: Both the supplied-normalization directional reduction and the full pool simulation extend to Massart label noise through a majority oracle that is correct outside the tolerance band. To avoid confusion with the geometric tolerance η \eta of Definition 3.4 , we write β \beta for the Massart flip rate. Theorem F.1 (Massart noise for directional search) . Under the supplied-normalization and full-support assumptions of Theorem D.24 , suppose each fresh label is independently flipped with conditional probability at most β < 1 / 2 \beta<1/2 . With probability at least 1 − δ 1-\delta , directional search achieves error ε \varepsilon using O ⁡ ( n ​ log ⁡ ( n ​ L / ε ) ​ log ⁡ ( n ​ log ⁡ ( n ​ L / ε ) / δ ) ( 1 − 2 ​ β ) 2 ) O\Bigl(\frac{n\log(nL/\varepsilon)\,\log(n\log(nL/\varepsilon)/\delta)}{(1-2\beta)^{2}}\Bigr) labels. Proof. Use the same target-independent precision γ \gamma as in Theorem D.24 . For each unit query q q , collect k k fresh points in its γ \gamma -neighborhood, where Q Q is a deterministic upper bound on the number of queries. If | ⟨ w , q ⟩ | > γ |\langle w,q\rangle|>\gamma , every selected point has the same clean label as q q , and conditional on the past and selected features, Hoeffding’s inequality makes the majority incorrect with probability at most δ / Q \delta/Q . For | ⟨ w , q ⟩ | ≤ γ |\langle w,q\rangle|\leq\gamma the majority may be arbitrary, which the imprecise comparator and imprecise binary search permit. A union bound over the adaptive transcript gives the oracle required by the noiseless proof. An angular cap of radius γ \gamma lies in the Euclidean γ \gamma -neighborhood and each fresh draw hits it with conditional probability at least a μ A ​ ( γ ) a_{\mu_{A}}(\gamma) . Corollary F.2 (Pool simulation under Massart noise) . Under the assumptions of Theorem 3.7 , suppose each label is independently flipped with conditional probability at most a known β < 1 / 2 \beta<1/2 , so that the clean target is Bayes optimal. With probability at least 1 − δ 1-\delta , a pool learner achieves excess error at most ε \varepsilon using O ⁡ ( n ​ log 3 ​ n ​ log 2 ​ n ε ​ δ ( 1 − 2 ​ β ) 2 ) O\Bigl(\frac{n\log^{3}n\,\log^{2}\frac{n}{\varepsilon\delta}}{(1-2\beta)^{2}}\Bigr) labels, uniformly over all such marginals and targets. The margin floor and the passive sample use no labels, and the passive sample is labeled by point location, not by querying it. Let Q = O ⁡ ( n ​ log 3 ​ n ​ log ⁡ ( N / δ ) ) Q=O(n\log^{3}n\log(N/\delta)) be the deterministic query bound of Proposition 3.6 , and k = ⌈ 2 ​ ( 1 − 2 ​ β ) − 2 ​ log ⁡ ( 4 ​ Q / δ ) ⌉ k=\lceil 2(1-2\beta)^{-2}\log(4Q/\delta)\rceil . To answer a query z ′ z^{\prime} in an instance ( V 0 , T ) (V_{0},T) , wait for k k fresh pool points p p with p p or − p -p within angle γ = η ∗ ​ θ 0 / κ ⁡ ( T ) \gamma=\eta^{*}\theta_{0}/\kappa(T) of T − 1 ​ z ′ T^{-1}z^{\prime} , request their labels, negate the labels of the reflected ones, and return the majority. A negated noisy label is the correct label of − p -p flipped with the same probability. If the query lies outside the tolerance band, then by Lemma 3.5 and the remark after it every one of these points, after negation where applicable, has the clean label sign ⁡ ⟨ z ′ , w ′ ⟩ \operatorname{sign}\langle z^{\prime},w^{\prime}\rangle , and conditional on the past and on the selected points the observed labels are independent and each is correct with probability at least 1 − β 1-\beta . Hoeffding’s inequality makes the majority wrong with probability at most δ / ( 4 ​ Q ) \delta/(4Q) . Inside the band any answer is allowed. A union bound over the at most Q Q queries shows that the majorities form an η ∗ \eta^{*} -subspace-relative oracle for the clean target with probability at least 1 − δ / 4 1-\delta/4 . Point location then labels the passive sample with clean labels, and a consistent halfspace has error at most ε \varepsilon against the clean target, hence excess error at most ε \varepsilon . The label count is Q ​ k Qk , and log ⁡ ( 4 ​ Q / δ ) = O ⁡ ( log ⁡ ( n / ( ε ​ δ ) ) ) \log(4Q/\delta)=O(\log(n/(\varepsilon\delta))) . ∎ Population Massart noise constrains the label bias at each point, whereas adversarial noise can concentrate precisely on the rare directions used by pool simulation. In particular, directional search may repeatedly query a region of angular mass far below ε \varepsilon , so it is not robust to adversarial noise. On classes for which the angular law is bounded above and below relative to a convex-body cone measure, radial randomization maps each point to its direction times an independent uniform-ball radius. Labels are unchanged, noise mass is preserved, and the resulting density is within a fixed factor of the uniform ball, so standard localized hinge-loss algorithms apply for sufficiently small adversarial noise. Agnostic and Tsybakov guarantees follow from disagreement-based theory wherever the disagreement coefficient admits a class-uniform bound, for example on the symmetric class with s > − 1 / n s>-1/n and on elliptical laws. An analogue of Theorem 3.7 under adversarial noise remains open ( Section 8 ). Imposing central symmetry does not by itself provide one.
