Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: arXiv.org perpetual non-exclusive license arXiv:2610.41001v1 [cs.LG] 29 Oct 2026 When Can Unlabeled Data Pools Replace Membership Queries? Dravyansh Sharma † † thanks: Most of the work was done while the author was at the Toyota Technological Institute at Chicago (TTIC). Affiliation: Microsoft Abstract Membership queries let a learner label arbitrary points and give near-optimal O ~ ​ ( n ​ log ⁡ ( 1 / ε ) ) 	ilde{O}(n\log(1/\varepsilon)) label complexity for halfspaces under every marginal. A pool learner may label only sampled points. We ask when unlabeled data can replace membership queries. For homogeneous halfspaces the answer depends only on the angular law of X / ‖ X ‖ X/\|X\| . If this law assigns zero mass to every hyperplane through the origin and positive mass to every nonempty open set of directions together with its reflection, a pool learner uses O ⁡ ( n ​ log 3 ​ n ​ log ⁡ ( n / ( ε ​ δ ) ) ) O(n\log^{3}n\log(n/(\varepsilon\delta))) labels, uniformly over all such marginals and targets, without density, moment, concavity or isotropy assumptions. The same label bound holds for non-homogeneous halfspaces under every marginal with full support and no mass on affine hyperplanes, including Gaussians. Dropping either angular assumption admits Ω ⁡ ( 1 / ε ) \Omega(1/\varepsilon) pool versus O ⁡ ( log ⁡ ( 1 / ε ) ) O(\log(1/\varepsilon)) membership-query separations, even with unlimited unlabeled data. The price is paid in unlabeled data: in dimension n ≥ 3 n\geq 3 , for every unlabeled budget fixed in advance, some marginal satisfying both assumptions forces Ω ⁡ ( 1 / ε ) \Omega(1/\varepsilon) labels. For isotropic s s -concave marginals in dimension n ≥ 3 n\geq 3 , unlimited pools keep logarithmic label rates for every finite s s . With an unlabeled budget fixed in advance, class-uniform polylogarithmic rates hold exactly for s > − 1 / ( n + 1 ) s>-1/(n+1) , or s > − 1 / n s>-1/n under central symmetry, and in the general class the optimal rate between these thresholds is Θ ~ ( ε − ( n − 2 ) / n ) 	ilde{\Theta}(\varepsilon^{-(n-2)/n}) . This extends the range s ≥ − 1 / ( 2 n + 3 ) s\geq-1/(2n+3) of previous sample-based guarantees, in the realizable setting. October 29, 2026 1 Introduction Membership queries are an unusually powerful form of active learning. The learner may choose any point and ask for its label. For halfspaces, point location , which labels every point of a given finite set under an unknown halfspace, can be done for a passive sample of size N N with O ⁡ ( n ​ log 2 ​ n ​ log ⁡ N ) O(n\log^{2}n\log N) synthesized queries ( Hopkins et al., 2020b ) , giving near-optimal membership-query learning under every marginal. An ordinary pool learner may only request labels of points it has sampled, and on worst-case finite point sets this can require Ω ⁡ ( N ) \Omega(N) labels ( Dasgupta, 2004 , Black et al., 2026 ) . For affine halfspaces under Gaussian marginals and a pool of m m points, Diakonikolas et al. (2024) prove an information-theoretic Ω ~ ​ ( n / ( ε ​ log ⁡ m ) ) 	ilde{\Omega}(n/(\varepsilon\log m)) lower bound. We ask the following distributional question (ignoring computational hardness). For which marginals can an unlabeled pool substitute for synthesized membership queries without increasing label complexity? We count two resources separately, namely labels and unlabeled examples , the latter meaning every sampled point the learner inspects. For halfspaces through the origin x ↦ sign ⁡ ⟨ w , x ⟩ x\mapsto\operatorname{sign}\langle w,xangle only the direction of a point matters, so the relevant object is the angular law μ = ℒ ⁡ ( X / ‖ X ‖ ) \mu=\mathcal{L}(X/\|X\|) , the distribution of the direction of X X . 1.1 Summary of Results Theorem 1.1 (Pools match membership queries in labels, Theorem 3.7 ) . Let n ≥ 2 n\geq 2 and let D D have no atom at the origin and an angular law that is hyperplane-null (it gives probability zero to every hyperplane through the origin) and has symmetric full support (every nonempty open set O O of directions has μ ⁡ ( O ∪ − O ) > 0 \mu(O\cup-O)>0 , which holds in particular if every nonempty open set of directions has positive probability, Section 2.2 ). A pool learner achieves error ε \varepsilon with probability 1 − δ 1-\delta using O ⁡ ( n ​ log 3 ​ n ​ log ⁡ n ε ​ δ ) O\Bigl(n\log^{3}n\,\log rac{n}{\varepsilon\delta}\Bigr) labels, uniformly over all such D D and all targets. This matches the Ω ⁡ ( n ​ log ⁡ ( 1 / ε ) ) \Omega(n\log(1/\varepsilon)) lower bound under the uniform distribution up to a log 3 ⁡ n \log^{3}n factor. The number of unlabeled examples is finite almost surely, necessarily depends on D D ( Theorem 1.3 ), and for our simulation is exponential in n n even for the uniform distribution ( Remark 3.11 ). Like the lower bounds below, Theorem 1.1 is information-theoretic. It counts labels and unlabeled examples, not running time ( Section C.2 ). The two assumptions can also be placed on different distributions. Error can be measured under a hyperplane-null law while labels come from points of a second law with symmetric full support, which may be atomic. The evaluation law itself must remain hyperplane-null ( Theorem 3.8 ). A simpler learner, directional search , approximates each membership query at a fixed angular resolution. It uses O ⁡ ( n ​ log ⁡ ( n / ρ μ − 1 ​ ( ε / 16 ) ) ) O(n\log(n/ho_{\mu}^{-1}(\varepsilon/16))) labels, where ρ μ − 1 ​ ( ε ) ho_{\mu}^{-1}(\varepsilon) is the largest width θ 	heta such that every band { u : | ⟨ u , w ⟩ | < θ } \{u:|\langle u,wangle|<	heta\} has μ \mu -mass at most ε \varepsilon ( Proposition 3.12 ). A mixture of three centered Gaussians makes this procedure’s label count arbitrarily large at fixed ε \varepsilon , even after an invertible linear change of coordinates ( Example 3.13 ). In contrast, Theorem 1.1 estimates query precision from unlabeled data and uses robust point location to confine its marginal dependence to the unlabeled cost. Theorem 1.2 (Both angular assumptions are necessary, Propositions 4.1 and 4.2 ) . For every ε \varepsilon there are two marginals, each depending on ε \varepsilon , for which every pool learner needs Ω ⁡ ( 1 / ε ) \Omega(1/\varepsilon) labels even with unlimited unlabeled data, while membership queries need O ⁡ ( log ⁡ ( 1 / ε ) ) O(\log(1/\varepsilon)) . The first is a smooth, centrally symmetric, hyperplane-null marginal on ℝ 3 \mathbb{R}^{3} without symmetric full support, with a finite family of targets. The second is a full-support marginal on ℝ 4 \mathbb{R}^{4} that charges a hyperplane, with a family of targets containing arbitrarily small tilts of one target, and there the lower bound holds in expectation. When both assumptions hold, pools recover the membership-query label rate, but the number of unlabeled examples in Theorem 1.1 depends on the marginal, and this dependence is unavoidable. Theorem 1.3 (Unlabeled cost cannot be uniform, Proposition 4.3 ) . Let n ≥ 3 n\geq 3 . For every unlabeled budget U ⁡ ( ε ) U(\varepsilon) , some marginal with a smooth, everywhere-positive, centrally symmetric density, so that both angular assumptions hold, forces every pool learner that inspects at most U ⁡ ( ε ) U(\varepsilon) examples to use Ω ⁡ ( 1 / ε ) \Omega(1/\varepsilon) labels, information-theoretically. For fixed n n this is the passive rate. Here the hard distribution may depend on the budget and on ε \varepsilon . We do not claim that a single distribution defeats every finite pool. Together with Theorem 1.1 , this shows that labels admit a bound uniform over the marginal class, whereas the number of unlabeled examples does not. Inside structured classes the same mechanism gives refined exponents. When homogeneous halfspaces act on a high-probability core as affine halfspaces of a lower-dimensional ball ( Definition 4.4 ), every finite budget forces Ω n ( ε − ( n − 2 ) / n ) \Omega_{n}(\varepsilon^{-(n-2)/n}) labels ( Theorem 4.5 ), which is tight for s s -concave marginals with − 1 / n < s ≤ − 1 / ( n + 1 ) -1/n<s\leq-1/(n+1) ( Section 5 ). Theorem 1.4 ( s s -concave marginals, Section 5 ) . For isotropic (mean zero, identity covariance) s s -concave marginals in dimension n ≥ 3 n\geq 3 ( Definition 5.1 , where s = 0 s=0 is log-concavity, and more negative s s allows heavier tails): (i) with an unlimited pool, O ⁡ ( n ​ log 3 ​ n ​ log ⁡ ( n / ( ε ​ δ ) ) ) O(n\log^{3}n\log(n/(\varepsilon\delta))) labels suffice for every finite s s ( Theorem 3.7 ), compared with the generic Ω ⁡ ( n ​ log ⁡ ( 1 / ε ) ) \Omega(n\log(1/\varepsilon)) lower bound; (ii) with an unlabeled budget fixed in advance for the class, polylogarithmic labels are achievable, via the disagreement-based learner CAL ( Cohn et al., 1994 ) and a class-uniform disagreement bound O n , s ​ ( log ⁡ ( 1 / ε ) ) O_{n,s}(\log(1/\varepsilon)) ( Section 2.3 ), if and only if s > − 1 / ( n + 1 ) s>-1/(n+1) , or s > − 1 / n s>-1/n in the centrally symmetric subclass ( f ⁡ ( x ) = f ⁡ ( − x ) f(x)=f(-x) ); (iii) for − 1 / n < s ≤ − 1 / ( n + 1 ) -1/n<s\leq-1/(n+1) in the general class, the worst-case disagreement coefficient is Θ n , s ( ε − ( n − 2 ) / n ) \Theta_{n,s}(\varepsilon^{-(n-2)/n}) , and Θ ~ n , s ( ε − ( n − 2 ) / n ) 	ilde{\Theta}_{n,s}(\varepsilon^{-(n-2)/n}) labels are necessary and sufficient with an unlabeled budget fixed in advance, at constant confidence; (iv) for s ≤ − 1 / n s\leq-1/n both the disagreement coefficient and the label count are Θ ⁡ ( 1 / ε ) \Theta(1/\varepsilon) , even in the symmetric subclass. Constants depend on n n and s s . In regime (ii) we prove no lower bound beyond Ω ⁡ ( n ​ log ⁡ ( 1 / ε ) ) \Omega(n\log(1/\varepsilon)) . All statements concern the realizable setting. Balcan and Zhang (2017) give polynomial-time, noise-tolerant learners for s ≥ − 1 / ( 2 n + 3 ) s\geq-1/(2n+3) . Theorem 1.4 is information-theoretic apart from the CAL implementation ( Corollary D.15 ). It locates the thresholds for class-uniform rates and the sharp rate between them, rather than extending their computational or noise guarantees. Item (i) follows from Theorem 3.7 . Items (ii)–(iv) use CAL and Lemma A.3 , with new arguments for the exponent in (iii) ( Section 5.1 ) and the symmetric construction in (iv) ( Lemma D.26 ). 1.2 Techniques A target-independent margin scale. A compactness argument implies that hyperplane-nullness is equivalent to the band mass ρ μ ​ ( θ ) = sup ‖ w ‖ = 1 μ ⁡ { u : | ⟨ u , w ⟩ | < θ } ho_{\mu}(	heta)=\sup_{\|w\|=1}\mu\{u:|\langle u,wangle|<	heta\} vanishing with θ 	heta ( Lemma 3.1 ). A uniform relative-deviation (VC) bound then finds, from unlabeled data alone, a width θ 0 > 0 	heta_{0}>0 (a margin floor ) with the following property. The learner draws an independent passive sample , an i.i.d. sample of size N = O ~ ​ ( n / ε ) N=	ilde{O}(n/\varepsilon) that it will label in full by point location, so that every consistent halfspace is ε \varepsilon -accurate. With high probability, every passive point has normalized margin at least θ 0 	heta_{0} from the fixed unknown target. No rate at which the band mass ρ μ ho_{\mu} vanishes is assumed, which is why labels are uniform while precision and unlabeled cost are not. This geometric margin is unrelated to the Tsybakov margin condition on label noise. Answering queries with pool points. The point-location algorithm of Hopkins et al. (2020b) repeatedly restricts to a subspace V V containing many sample points and applies a linear map T T that puts those points in approximately isotropic position (their second-moment matrix becomes nearly a multiple of the identity). Every such subspace contains a passive point, which lower-bounds the norm of the projected target. Hence a pool point within angle γ \gamma of a requested direction (or of its antipode, with the label negated) returns the correct label unless the transformed query q q has relative margin | ⟨ q , w ′ ⟩ | / ( ‖ q ‖ ​ ‖ w ′ ‖ ) |\langle q,w^{\prime}angle|/(\|q\|\|w^{\prime}\|) at most γ ​ κ ​ ( T ) / θ 0 \gamma\kappa(T)/	heta_{0} with respect to the transformed target normal w ′ w^{\prime} , where κ ⁡ ( T ) = ‖ T ‖ ​ ‖ T − 1 ‖ \kappa(T)=\|T\|\|T^{-1}\| is the condition number ( Lemma 3.5 ). Because the learner chooses γ \gamma after seeing T T , the pool answers form a subspace-relative oracle ( Definition 3.4 ). This is stronger than a single margin-tolerant oracle in fixed coordinates, and it is what robust point location needs. Robust point location. We modify Hopkins et al. (2020b) to tolerate such an oracle. Their margin comparisons already carry multiplicative slack. The one step that needs exact comparisons is deterministic median selection, which we replace by a round-robin tournament robust to near-ties, and we enlarge one acceptance threshold. This costs one log ⁡ n \log n factor ( Proposition 3.6 ). Table 2 lists, with their hypotheses, all results of Hopkins et al. (2020b) that we use. Hard instances for the lower bounds. The lower bounds place the informative directions in a region of vanishing mass. In the general s s -concave class, a rare tail moves the mean, while a high-probability core is, after a projective change of coordinates, a uniform ball. In the symmetric class, successive logarithmic radial scales are dominated by different norms, so the angular law can approximate a mixture of the angular laws of elongated ellipsoids. Relation to prior work. The angular law (radially symmetric marginals were already exploited for origin-centered separators by Kearns 1998 ), exponential active improvements, pool-versus-synthesis gaps, and the splitting-index distinction between how informative a query is and how likely the unlabeled distribution is to produce it ( Dasgupta, 2005 , Hanneke, 2014 ) are all classical. That a sufficiently rich pool approximates membership queries is folklore. The infinite full-support pool limit is discussed in Gonen et al. (2013) , and Diakonikolas et al. (2024) remark that pools approach membership queries as they grow exponentially. Dasgupta’s label bounds carry logarithmic factors that depend on the marginal, as does the directional search of Proposition 3.12 . Our contributions are threefold. Theorem 3.7 removes every marginal-dependent factor from the label count. We show that both angular assumptions are needed. Finally, we show that the remaining marginal dependence, in unlabeled data, cannot be removed ( Theorem 1.3 ). Prior robustness guarantees. The guarantees of Hopkins et al. (2020b) allow the algorithm itself to fail with small probability (their “bounded-error” and “reliable” notions refer to this failure probability), but they assume every query is answered correctly. Their companion work with comparison queries ( Hopkins et al., 2020a ) handles stochastic bounded (Massart) label noise rather than arbitrary answers inside a relative-margin band. The closest model is the unreliable boundary queries of Blum et al. (1995) , where membership queries near the boundary may be answered wrongly and the distribution puts no mass there, but their goal is polynomial-time PAC learning of specific classes rather than near-optimal query complexity for all halfspaces. We are not aware of a near-optimal point-location algorithm with guarantees in this setting. Since a nearby sampled direction can be wrong deterministically, majority votes do not help. Our modifications. The isotropic-transform arguments of Hopkins et al. (2020b) , which rest on the theorems of Forster (2002) and Barthe (1998) , and their matrix-concentration, structural and boosting arguments do not involve the oracle. Appendix B checks the hypotheses of each result we use under the new oracle. Only three oracle-sensitive steps change. Comparison. | m ⁡ ( a ) | |m(a)| and | m ⁡ ( b ) | |m(b)| are compared via the signs of a a , b b and a signed difference, which is correct whenever the magnitudes differ by more than the tolerance-induced error ( Lemma B.1 ). Selection. Deterministic median selection is fragile under such a comparator, so StructureSearch instead compares all pairs in a small representative set and picks a middle win count, which controls the rank of the selected representative from both sides up to one comparator error ( Lemma B.2 ). This is the classical paired-comparison method in the bounded-error model of Ajtai et al. (2015) , and it costs one extra log ⁡ n \log n factor. Dimension reduction. DimReduce accepts a sampled subset when its representative’s margin is small relative to a scaled reference point, tested with three sign queries, and spurious accepted subsets only add positive semidefinite terms to the covariance estimate ( Hopkins et al., 2020b , Lemma 4.15) .
